Module 1 · AI-assisted software development

AI-assisted software development

How much of the work you give to the AI.

~10 seconds. Say the name and move. This is deliberately the first thing after the poll: the room has just put its hands up for autocomplete, chat, terminal agent or delegation, and those are the four levels on the next two slides. Name them while the tally is still on the board.

Connects toThe two slides that follow are the whole section: what each level looks like at the keyboard, then the abstraction over them. Module 2 is this section done slowly, for a whole day.

1 · AI-assisted software development

Four ways to work with AI

Level What the AI produces What you check
1autocomplete A line or a few lines Each suggestion, as it appears
2chat in the editor A function, a class or a test Each piece, before you use it
3agent, you approve A task across several files Each change and command
4agent works alone A whole feature, start to finish The plan and the pull request
Click to see each level
editor · inline suggestion
editor · chat fills the body
terminal · accept every diff
terminal · auto-accept on

~3 min. The rows reveal one at a time, on click or on the arrow key, and the panel on the right switches to a mockup of that level as it appears. Reveal a level, let the loop run twice, then talk over it.

The pair to dwell on is 3 against 4. At level 3 you type "y" over and over and it never finishes; at level 4 it lands four changes in two seconds and hands you one pull request. That is the whole trade, visible: level 3 costs your attention on every change, level 4 costs you the ability to see any of them one by one.

How each level fails, since it is not on the slide and it is the part the room has opinions about. 1: plausible lines you accept while thinking about something else. 2: code that fits the prompt and not the codebase around it. 3: you approve twenty changes and stop reading properly at eight. 4: a large, tidy, confident change built on a wrong assumption made in minute two. Ask which of those they recognise from their own week.

Connects toThe failure modes behind these levels are 2.6's syllabus. Blast radius and where the seams sit is 2.3.

1 · AI-assisted software development

The more you hand over, the less you read

~3 min. Straight after the mockups, so walk down the rows once and land the claim in the caption. The point people miss: your reading capacity is fixed. Autonomy does not give you more of it, it just relocates it.

They have just seen all four at the keyboard, so this slide is the abstraction over them: same four levels, and now what actually changes. Levels 3 and 4 are the ones the rest of the day is about. Modules 2.6 and 2.7 come back to the fact that review is the bottleneck and adding agents does not remove it.

If someone challenges the amber: they are right to. It is not “code that landed unreviewed”. At level 3 every change is approved before it lands, so the amber is what the agent did between changes, the files it opened, the commands it ran, the paths it tried and abandoned. You never read that, and it is where a wrong assumption gets established. At level 4 the amber is the work itself.

This is the diagram to reuse whenever someone asks where in the day we are.

Connects to2.6 is the level 3 bottleneck in full, 2.7 is worktrees and parallel agents at level 4, and 2.8 names the frameworks built on top of these levels.

Module 1 · Vibes vs. Engineering

Vibes vs. Engineering

How much you check, and what decides it.

~10 seconds. Say the name and move. The point of putting a divider here is that the room has just spent six minutes on how much you hand over, and the next idea is a different axis entirely. The pause is the signal.

Connects toThe slide that follows, and through it to 2.2, 2.5, 2.6 and Module 3, which are the four things the right-hand end of that scale is made of.

1 · Vibes vs. Engineering

How much you check is a separate choice

Two separate choices: how much you hand over, and how much you check.

Stay left for throwaway code. Move right when it’s unfamiliar, hard to undo, or someone has to answer for it.

~2 min. Point at the poll tally from the opener here. The room will read the right-hand end as “the grown-up one”, so say plainly that the left end is a legitimate place to work and that most people's best AI experiences happened there, on something disposable.

The two boxes are the whole slide, and they reveal on click, one each. Let the scale sit on its own first, then bring in the left box, then the right. The line to say as the second one lands: same mode, both ends, and the only difference is what was around it. It is deliberately not written on the slide, so the picture makes the point before you do. That is the answer to “is letting the agent work alone dangerous”, which someone always asks: handing over a lot is not the risk on its own; handing over a lot and checking little is.

Where they get it wrong in practice: they will vibe-code a prototype, it works, and then the prototype goes to production without ever moving right on this scale. That is worth naming out loud, because it is the most common way this ends badly and nobody decided to do it.

Connects toEverything on the right of this scale is the rest of the day: the spec is 2.2, the tests are 2.5, reading every diff is 2.6, and the gates are Module 3. “Hard to reverse” is the judgement 2.3 makes about seams.

How it works

What happens inside these AI tools.

~10 seconds. A breath, not a slide. Say the section name and move.

1 · How it works

Prompting is not engineering

Same input, same build. Same prompt, different code.

“It worked when I tried it” is not a test.

~1.5 min. Talk from the picture, not from the words. Do not turn this into an LLM lecture, KBC's own prerequisite webinar covers the fundamentals. Walk the top lane, then the bottom lane, and let the three different diffs do the arguing.

The title is a claim, so make it. Prompt engineering is the phrase everyone in the room arrives with, and this slide says it is not engineering in the sense they mean. Engineering is exact, specific and reproducible: same input, same artifact, and you can put a hash on it. Prompting has none of those properties, and no amount of care makes them appear.

Say the diffs are illustrative, and that the shape is the point: not that the runs are bad, but that they are different. Any one of those three diffs might be fine. You cannot tell which one you are going to get.

There is no live demo in this module, so this picture is doing the work on its own. Fix that cheaply: run the same prompt twice on the lab repo before the session and bring the two diffs as screenshots. Showing them here is the difference between a claim and a fact. The next slide is why it happens.

The kicker is the hinge of the whole day. If what has to hold every time has to be checked every time, then the rest of the module is about where that checking lives, and Modules 2 and 3 are where you put it. Say it slowly, it is the sentence the day hangs on.

Connects to2.5 builds the verification loops this slide argues for, 2.6 is the human half of the checking, and Module 3 is the half that runs without anyone remembering.

1 · How it works

What the model actually does

Would you notice if this run did it differently?

~1.5 min. Talk from the picture, not from bullets. Two things to point at: the height of the first bar, which is why it usually looks right, and the tail, which is where “it said something strange” comes from.

Say the numbers are illustrative. They are made up to show the shape. Do not quote them as measured.

If someone asks about temperature: it sharpens or flattens these bars, and in most coding tools you do not get to set it. Worth adding that even greedy decoding is not a guarantee of repeatability here, because the repo, the tool results and the file contents differ between runs, so the input differs too.

If someone wants the architecture: offer it at the break. This slide is here to justify one supervision habit, not to teach transformers.

Connects to2.2 is this slide's consequence: leave a gap and the most likely token fills it from training data. 2.4 is what happens to these probabilities when the window fills up.

1 · How it works

Nothing is remembered

No memory between messages. Each one resends the whole conversation.

~2 min. This is the slide for a room of developers: they think in requests, so show them the requests. Walk down the arrows, then point at the bottom one and say the quiet part, that the payload grows with everything that already happened, not with the work still to do.

Three things to say over the picture: long sessions get more expensive and less accurate at the same time, because everything in the window competes for attention. There is no learning across sessions, so a correction you made an hour ago is gone unless somebody wrote it into the repo. And the unchanging system-and-tools prefix on every arrow is why prompt caching exists, which is also why reordering your rule files invalidates it.

Do not go deeper than the picture. If someone asks about compaction or context editing, that is 2.4, and Module 4 does memory and retrieval.

Connects to2.1 is the files that survive the session, 2.4 is managing the window and writing handovers, 2.7 is tracking work across sessions, and Module 4 is memory and retrieval as the paid alternative.

1 · How it works

Thinking vs. reasoning vs. effort

Thinking = reasoning: working the problem before answering. Effort sets how much (/effort in Claude Code).

Task
Effort
Thinking
0 tokens
Result —

Made-up numbers. Simple tasks stop improving long before the cost stops rising.

Settle the vocabulary in one breath. They will hear all three words this year and assume they are three features. Thinking and reasoning are the same mechanism under two vendor names; effort is the only one of the three that is a control you set.

~2 min. Run it live: leave the task on rename a field and walk the effort dial from low to max. The result line never changes and the token count goes up about sixty times. Then switch to choose a retry strategy and walk it again, where the result does change, and stops changing between xhigh and max.

What we tested, and what we found. This slide started from review feedback that reasoning models overthink simple tasks. We tried it: one constant to change, at max effort. It did not pad the answer with unnecessary scaffolding, so do not tell the room that high effort makes the answer bigger. What it did instead was change the constant correctly and then rewrite the tests, unasked, to assert against the constant rather than literal values. Green suite, and it can no longer detect a wrong threshold at all.

When someone says that is just DRY, and they will: concede most of it. Those tests still catch a flipped boundary and a wrong discount rate; they are blind to exactly one thing, the value of the threshold, which is the one number the ticket was about. The tell is the motivation: constant-relative assertions were available before the task too. The refactor happened because a test went red, not because anyone judged it better, and a change that only becomes attractive when it silences a failure is worth a second look. Settle it by mutating rather than arguing, which is the habit worth leaving them with.

Do not attribute that to the effort level yet. We have no low-effort comparison, so we do not know whether the level caused it. If asked, that is the honest answer. The claim this slide makes stays the narrow one: on mechanical work the answer stops improving long before the spend stops climbing.

The takeaway is not “use low effort”. It is that the level is a property of the task. Coding and long-horizon agentic work genuinely repay high effort; classification, chat and high-volume routes usually do not. xhigh is the Claude Code default for that reason.

Do not put cost figures on this slide. Team decision on 28 Aug: cost-per-result benchmarks are hand-wavy and go stale. If the room presses for real numbers, open the vendor's current pricing page on the day and say that is what you are doing.

Click a chip again, or press R, to replay the animation.

Connects to2.2 is where high effort pays, on the alignment conversation. 2.4 is attention pressure, the other reason more tokens is not more quality. Module 4 does cost and routing work to smaller models.

1 · How it works

Effort is also initiative

Effort isn’t only for hard tasks. It sets how much the model decides and does on its own.

  • EffortGood forWhat it does unasked
  • lowsketchesa quick starting point, you stay in the loop
  • mediumfeaturesthe task, done reasonably
  • highbug fixesreproduces the bug, reviews its draft, adds tests
  • maxautonomousextra features, and assumptions made for you

Vague prompt + high effort = more decisions you didn’t make.

Source: “Using Claude Code: Spending your effort”, Thariq Shihipar

~1.5 min. Four clicks for the rows, then the kicker. The previous slide framed effort as difficulty. This one adds the other half: initiative.

The example to tell: the same underspecified prompt, “build a fitness app”. At low effort (about 1.5 min) it produced a log and a simple graph. At max (about 67 min) it added more detail and a heat chart nobody asked for. Each level up made more choices on the user’s behalf.

With a detailed spec, the levels converge. The outputs looked much more alike, and at max it even simplified some details. That is the argument for 2.2: pin the decisions down and effort goes into checking, not inventing.

Where high effort pays: missed edge cases. In the article’s runs, “missed a case” failures fell from 59 to 24 between low and max. Wrong-approach failures barely moved (133 to 107). More effort checks harder; it does not pick a better approach.

The suggested loop: spec and interview first, implement and iterate at low effort, then verify and test at high effort.

Connects to2.2’s conversation before the code, which removes the decisions high effort would otherwise make for you. 2.5 is the verification high effort is good at.

1 · How it works

Models have personalities

Same prompt, different model, different idea of the job.

  • ModelStyleWhat to do about it
  • GPTsteriledoes what you said, nothing more. Ask for the extras.
  • Opusopinionatedassumes what you want and adds it. Say what’s out of scope.

Switching models? Re-check your prompts.

Our experience, not a benchmark. Behaviour shifts between versions.

~1 min. Two clicks, then the kicker. This builds on the previous slide: effort sets how much initiative a model takes, and the model itself sets its default.

Make it concrete: ask both for “add a retry to the payment call”. GPT tends to add the retry and stop. Opus tends to add the retry, plus backoff, logging, a config flag and a refactor it thought you would like. Neither is wrong; they answer different questions.

Ask the room: who has switched tools and found their old prompts stopped working? That is this slide.

Keep it honest. This is what we see day to day, not a measured result, and it changes with every model release. The habit to leave them with is to re-test prompts and rules files when the model changes, not to memorise which model does what.

Connects to the exercise later in this module, where they pick a model per task. 2.2 pins the scope down so the model’s defaults matter less.

1 · How it works

Meta prompting

Ask the model to rewrite your prompt before it does the task.

  • What would an expert do that I didn’t ask for?
  • What raw material would they start from?
  • Which methods and tools would they use?
  • What, besides me, would prove it’s right?

Deeper, not bigger. Read the new prompt before you run it.

Source: Felix Rieseberg, “How to be more ambitious: a tutorial for humans with models”

~1.5 min. Four clicks for the questions, then the kicker. Give a live example: “My task is: add retries to the payment call. Answer these four questions, then rewrite my prompt.” A good rewrite asks for retries that never charge twice, starts from the real failure logs, and proves it with a failing test.

The idea in one sentence: the model often knows more about how an expert would do the task than your prompt asks for, so ask it to write the better prompt, then run that one. It is the cheapest way to raise the ambition of a request.

Question four matters most. It moves the check out of the model and into something that can fail, like a test. That ties back to “Prompting is not engineering”: what has to hold every time has to be checked every time.

Do not oversell it. The rewritten prompt still needs your review. It can add work nobody asked for, or confidently assume a rule that is wrong for your system.

Source: Felix Rieseberg, “How to be more ambitious: a tutorial for humans with models”, October 2026 (felixrieseberg.com). The four questions are adapted from his.

Connects to2.2 takes this further with a conversation before the code, where the model asks you the questions. 2.5 builds the tests that question four asks for.

1 · Vocabulary

What an agent is made of

Five parts. What matters is when each is sent to the model.

  • PartSent to the modelWhat it is
  • rules fileevery messageteam rules
  • skillwhen relevantinstructions for an occasional task
  • subagentwhen askeda helper that works apart and reports back
  • MCP serverevery messagea link to outside tools and data
  • hooknevera script that runs at set moments

every message means you pay for it every message.

~1.5 min. A primer, not a lesson. Nobody should reach the next slide's table not knowing what a skill is. Resist teaching any of it properly, because 2.1 does all five hands-on and you will run out of day.

The “loads” column is the whole slide. It ties straight back to the request diagram: the always-loaded pieces are the part of every request you pay for whether or not it is relevant. That is the sentence to say.

If someone asks how a skill gets chosen: the agent reads a one-line description and judges whether it matches, or you invoke it by name. It can miss, and it will not tell you it missed. Say that is 2.1's problem and move on.

Connects to2.1 teaches all five on the lab repo, the Controls slide already showed the hook, and Module 4 takes MCP and subagents to depth. Backwards, it lands on the request diagram two slides back.

Module 1 · SDLC

The SDLC

Coding is only the middle. AI changes the steps around it too.

~10 seconds. Say the name and move. Everything so far has been about the part of the day where code gets written. This section is the reminder that the same shift is happening either side of it, and that the question of how much to hand over does not stop at the edges of the editor.

Three real systems follow, one client PoC before the code and two after it. This is the only part of the module that shows something running rather than a diagram, which is why it survived the cut that took the live demo out.

The line to land at the end of the section: an agent that opens a pull request off an alert is level 4 with production as the trigger, so it gets the same scrutiny as any other level 4 work. Handing over does not stop at merge.

1 · SDLC

AI at every step: a client prototype

From first meeting to final presentation.

AI saves time before the code too. Today covers the last two boxes.

~2 min. One click, for the two brackets. Walk the six stages first, then reveal the brackets and say the kicker. The whole point of the slide is the bracket on the left: four stages of real client delivery that happened before any code existed.

No caption on this figure, on purpose. It said “three people, three streams, one shared workflow”, which is worth knowing and worth saying out loud, but it is engagement detail and it does not belong on a slide. Do not put a caption back.

Provenance, and a caveat. A client-facing PoC delivered at a hackathon. The six stages and their tools are taken from that engagement's own process deck, and worth checking against its business-value deck before delivery. Do not name the client, in the room or in the notes.

The stage to dwell on is step one. Meeting notes as a first-class input, not a courtesy. Requirements and stories in step two are generated from what step one captured, which is why a gap in the notes becomes a gap in the spec, and then a gap the agent fills with the most likely thing.

Steps three and four are the ones a room of developers will not expect. Architecture design and BPMN/UML diagrams, the latter through custom skills rather than a general prompt. That is the same mechanism as 2.1: a procedure written down once, loaded when it matches.

Do not oversell it. It was a hackathon, so nothing here was under production constraints, and the honest framing is that this is the left-hand end of the verification scale done well, not proof that the right-hand end works this way.

Open question, resolve before delivery: whether KBC permits meeting capture over internal calls at all, and by which vendor. Step one names Granola on the slide, so somebody has to confirm that is fine to show.

Connects to2.2 is the spec conversation, which is step two done slowly. 2.1 is the custom skills in step four. Steps five and six are Modules 2 and 3, which is what the kicker means by the last two boxes.

1 · SDLC

Our own R&D: a data platform that fixes itself

One rule shapes the whole design: the model never gets to act on its own.

~2 min. Ours, so you can be candid about it. The one sentence to say is the lead, verbatim: everything in that codebase follows from the constraint that the language model never has power. Then trace the diagram once, and land on the crossed-out arrow.

Why it belongs in this deck. It is the right-hand end of the verification scale, built out: the model produces a hypothesis, and every part that can actually change something is deterministic, typed and tested. That is the honest answer to “so do we just let it loose in production”, and it is more convincing than the scale slide because it is a real system rather than a diagram.

The autonomy dial is the callback. Shadow, approval-gated, autonomous. The same four levels of handing over, in production, with the leash length as a config value per playbook rather than a habit. If you only have time for one point on this slide, make it that one.

Numbers if the room wants them: 19 typed actions, 10 playbooks with graduated autonomy, 34 architecture decision records, and promotion between autonomy levels gated on classification accuracy, recovery rate, rollback rate and reopened-incident rate.

Be honest about maturity. Validated on the development estate. Production scale and private networking are not tested yet. Say so unprompted, because someone will ask and the credibility of the whole slide rests on not overselling it.

Connects toThe right-hand end of Vibes vs. Engineering, made real. Module 3 is the gate layer this depends on.

1 · SDLC

After release: from a fixed script to an agent

A production test fails. What changes is how much a person does.

~2.5 min. Two clicks: the loop, then the dashed row. Walk the top row and let it dead-end, then the middle row, then reveal the loop and say the line — that arrow is the entire difference between a workflow with an agentic step and an agent. Then the dashed row for where it goes.

This is the post-delivery slide, so frame it that way. Nothing here is triggered by a developer opening a ticket. It starts with a test failing on real data, at whatever hour that happens, which is a different problem from writing the code in the first place. The question of how much to hand over does not stop at merge, and this is the concrete proof.

What the old system actually was. Open Metadata, a Chainlit chat front end, a dbt repo and Athena. dbt tests flagged the failures, results were pushed to Open Metadata as JSON, and the workflow handed the model a pre-assembled context. It did generate and run one query against Athena, which is the “agentic step”, and that is exactly where it stopped: no retry, no second look, no verification.

Why the new one is better, precisely. Not because the model got smarter. Because the context is curated, kept in S3 as skills and files the agent reads on demand, and because it can run a query, read the answer and decide what to ask next. That is the same claim the How it works section made about what goes into the window.

The dashed row is the honest part. Today it is still triggered by hand, so a failure at 02:00 waits for a human to notice. Firing on the failure and mailing the analyst the first diagnosis is on the table; proposing the fix rather than stopping at a diagnosis comes after that. Say plainly that the dashes mean not built, because the credibility of the other two rows depends on it.

Check the rest of the detail with Arno too — he owns the current setup. In particular confirm it is fair to present this as the room's own system; if not, introduce it as a client example.

Connects toThe loop is the move from level 3 to level 4 in AI-assisted software development, applied to an incident instead of a feature. The curated context is 2.1. The dashed row is Module 3's problem: what gates a fix nobody asked for.

Module 1 · Exercise

Exercise time

Which model, and how much effort?

~10 seconds. Say the name, ask the question, then stop. The room has just seen the effort slide and the three worked examples, so the question should already feel concrete.

Three slides, in this order: three tasks, which they argue from instinct; then the three questions that decide it; then what we would pick. Argue first, tool second. The questions land harder once the room has noticed it disagrees with itself.

Say this on the way in: nobody hands you the setting. There is no house default that is right for everything, because the right answer changes per task.

Connects toThinking vs. reasoning vs. effort, which showed the dial. This exercise is when to turn it. 2.2 comes back to it with planning versus implementing.

1 · Exercise

Three tasks

Pick a model and effort for each. Go with your gut.

01

Upgrade a library in 60 files

  • the same mechanical change in every file
  • the compiler and tests catch most slips
  • the first file needs a few real decisions

model? effort?

02

A payment that is sometimes charged twice

  • about once a week, and nobody can reproduce it
  • you have the logs from the last three cases
  • real money, real customers

model? effort?

03

Sort 2,000 support tickets every night

  • eight categories, a few lines per ticket
  • runs on its own at 02:00
  • a wrong label sends a ticket to the wrong team

model? effort?

Models: small and fast · mid-size · largest    Effort: low · medium · high · max

~3 min. Three clicks, one card each. Reveal a card, take a show of hands for the model, then for the effort, and ask one person from each side why. Do not give answers here; they are two slides on.

The third bullet on each card is the one that turns the answer. If someone answers from the title alone, ask them to read the last bullet out loud.

Where the room usually goes wrong. 01: they pick one setting for the whole job, either the largest model at max for all 60 files or the cheapest for all of it, including the first file that needs the decisions. 02: they assume max effort will find the bug. It will not without the logs and a way to reproduce it. 03: they pick the model they chat with every day, because it is the one they know.

Keep the tiers generic on the slide. If someone asks for names: in Claude Code the three tiers are Haiku, Sonnet and Opus, chosen with /model, and effort is /effort. Copilot has a model picker per chat. The names change every few months; the tiers do not.

No cost figures. Same team decision as the effort slide (28 Aug): prices go stale. Talk about cost in relative terms only.

Connects toThe effort slide in How it works, where the answer on the simple task stopped improving long before the cost did. The next slide is the three questions that decide these.

1 · Exercise

What decides it

Three questions, in this order.

  • Hard, or just long? Connected decisions earn a stronger model. Repetition doesn’t.
  • Would you notice a mistake? If tests catch it, go cheap. If not, pay for quality.
  • How often does it run? Once: spend freely. 2,000 times a night: every token counts.

Effort can’t add missing information. No logs, no fix.

~2 min. Four clicks: three questions, then the kicker. Take the card the room split on most and run it through the questions out loud, one question per click. That beats explaining them in the abstract.

Question one is the one people skip. They judge by size. Sixty files sounds big, so it gets the big model. But sixty copies of one easy edit is volume, and volume is what small models are for.

Question two is about checks, not about stakes alone. The library upgrade touches production code too, but the compiler and the tests tell you within minutes when it is wrong. The double charge has nothing like that, which is why it gets the expensive answer.

The kicker is the line to land. Effort is thinking time, not knowledge. It cannot read logs it was never given, or know a decision nobody wrote down. That is the bridge into 2.1.

Connects to2.2's slide on planning versus implementing, which is question one applied to a single feature. 2.1 is the kicker: getting the right information in front of the model in the first place.

1 · Exercise

What we would pick

Task Model Effort Why Watch out for
01library upgrade largest, then small high, then low One set of decisions, then 59 edits the compiler checks. Paying for one decision 60 times.
02charged twice largest high to max Subtle bug, real money, no signal when it’s wrong. Effort isn’t evidence. Give it the logs; get a failing test first.
03ticket sorting small and fast low Easy per ticket; the job is volume. Test on 200 hand-sorted tickets. Defaulting to your chat model. Escalate unsure tickets.

Starting points, not rules. Try two settings and compare.

~3 min. Three clicks, one row each. Say the model and effort, then the “watch out for” column, which is where the learning is. Do not defend the picks too hard; a room that argues with them is doing the exercise.

01 is two settings, not one. That is the surprise for most of the room. Make the decisions once with a strong model on the first file, write them down as the pattern, then let a fast model repeat it. It is the same split as planning versus implementing in 2.2.

02: max is defensible. If someone argues for max instead of high, agree. The point is the right-hand column: the most capable model at max effort, without the logs, will produce a confident and plausible wrong answer. Ask for a test that reproduces the double charge before anyone accepts a fix.

03: measuring is the point. Nobody can tell whether a small model is good enough by looking at it. Two hundred tickets someone already sorted by hand gives you a number in ten minutes. If the number is too low, move up one size, not straight to the largest.

If someone asks why not use the largest model for everything: it is slower and it costs more on every call, and on easy work the answer does not get better. That is the effort slide again, applied to the model instead of the dial.

Connects toBackwards, the three cards and the effort slide in How it works. Forwards, 2.2 on planning versus implementing and Module 4 on what a tool costs to run.

1 · Handoff

Next: what the agent knows at the start of a session

Three takeaways.

  • Decide per task: what to hand over, which model and effort, what catches mistakes.
  • Nothing is remembered: write down what the next session needs.
  • Checking has to happen somewhere, and less of it can be you.

2.1 picks up point two: project files that give every session the same start.

~1 min. Hard stop at 10:00, 2.1 is hands-on and needs its full thirty minutes. If you are over, cut this slide and say the three lines while people open their lab environment.

1 · Caching

KV caching

Without a cache: France

01 / 06

Every input token passes through the model to predict “Paris”.

Words and punctuation stand in for tokens. Prompt processing is slowed down for illustration.

Right / Space: next step · Left: previous step · R: restart

Six manual steps: uncached France, uncached Belgium, cache-building France, Belgium prefix lookup, load the shared prefix, and compute Belgium's new suffix. Each step plays once and holds. Pause and Replay step control the current animation. Right or Space advances, Left goes back, and R restarts all six steps. Reduced motion shows completed states.

The prompts are What is the capital of France? and What is the capital of Belgium? Paris and Brussels are newly predicted answers. Words and punctuation stand in for token units, hashes are illustrative short labels, and three layers stand in for a full model. Real tokenization can split words. Chat template tokens are omitted. This short example does not imply a commercial API cache hit or minimum cache length.

The forward signal is an illustration of activations passing through a causal transformer. Prompt prefill normally processes many positions in parallel; the sequential word animation slows this down for teaching. Signals move forward through fixed weights. This is inference, with no training or weight updates.

KV caching stores token-derived key and value vectors at each attention layer. Within generation, the model reuses earlier keys and values when it processes a new token. It still calculates new queries and attends to earlier keys and values. These are not cached model weights, attention scores, or a single final network state. Reference: https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/cache_explanation

The cross-request hash lookup is prompt or prefix caching built on the KV cache, so this example shows both mechanisms. Cumulative hashes include the preceding prefix and current token IDs, together with relevant model and request context. Real implementations may index complete multi-token blocks and only reuse matching block boundaries. The single-unit entries are a teaching simplification. Reference: https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/design/prefix_caching/

Only What is the capital of matches. Belgium differs from France. The following question mark also needs recomputation because its preceding context differs, even though the same punctuation occurs in the first prompt. Arbitrary matching substrings cannot be reused as if they were identical prefixes.

Loading the prefix makes its saved keys and values available at every attention layer. Belgium and the question mark still pass through all layers and attend to the cached prefix. The cache does not jump to a later network layer or restore weights. The three green ports represent per-layer cache access; a serving engine may reuse memory references without physically copying data.

1 · Caching

Caching trade-offs

  • Faster responses and lower costsReuse earlier computation. A response cache returns the whole answer.
  • More memory and storageLong contexts use more KV memory. The context window doesn’t grow.
  • Saved answers can become outdatedResponse caches can repeat stale answers. KV caching still generates fresh.
  • Extra work to keep the cache validTrack hits, expiry and cost. Scope responses to the right user.

Right / Space: reveal next point · Left: previous step · R: restart

Reveal the four bullets in order. These costs and benefits apply differently to the related cache layers: prompt caching can reuse KV state across requests, while response caching stores the complete output. Speed and cost savings depend on reuse.

KV caching avoids recalculating earlier attention keys and values. Storing per-token, per-layer vectors consumes memory; long contexts and many concurrent requests increase that demand. The exact memory growth depends on the architecture and cache strategy. A cache does not expand the model's context window. Source: https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/cache_explanation

Prompt caching saves work on a matching prefix, but a cache miss still requires computation and each response still requires generation. Edits early in a prompt can invalidate later prefix reuse. Cache entries may expire or be evicted. Minimum sizes, write charges, and retention differ by provider. Judge total savings from actual reuse rather than assuming every request benefits. Source: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching

Response caching can avoid a whole inference call. It also repeats a saved mistake, freezes output variation, and may return an outdated answer when external facts change. Include all relevant request context and model settings in the key, isolate user or tenant data where needed, and choose an expiry or invalidation policy. Semantic similarity adds a separate risk of reusing an answer for a question that is only superficially similar. Exact lookup key reference: https://reference.langchain.com/python/langchain-core/caches/BaseCache/lookup

For outdated answers, use the travel assistant as an example: a capital city answer usually changes slowly, a forecast changes frequently, and a booking status can change immediately after an action. Response caching must not skip a required booking or ticket operation. Revalidate live state when the task requires it. These are teaching examples rather than fixed cache lifetimes. Freshness reference: https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/use-cases/cache-aside/

All cache layers add storage or lookup overhead and require lifecycle management. Measure hit rate, end-to-end latency, memory usage, total cost, and correctness. A workload with little reusable content may gain little from cross-request caching.

1 · Caching

Prompt order for caching

  • Stable content at the topSystem prompt, instructions, tools, examples.
  • Changing content at the bottomFresh context, tool results, the latest question.
  • Keep the shared prefix identicalAn early edit breaks reuse from there on.

Right / Space: reveal next point · Left: previous step · R: restart

This follows from prefix caching: unchanged tokens at the beginning are candidates for reuse. Keep stable instructions and reusable examples early, then append request-specific material later.

For the travel assistant, keep the role, tool-use instructions, and output format stable. Put the current destination, fresh research, weather results, and latest user request later in their appropriate message positions. Avoid injecting a changing timestamp or request ID before otherwise reusable content.

Preserve message roles, instruction priority, and chronological conversation order. This is a principle for constructing the request, not a reason to move untrusted tool output into the system prompt or reorder tool results. The provider may place tool definitions before system instructions in its serialized prefix.

Matching means the same token prefix, not merely equivalent wording. Changing an early token prevents reuse of later cached positions that depend on it. Provider block boundaries can shorten the reusable prefix further.

Ordering supports cache reuse but does not guarantee a cache hit. Minimum lengths, retention, model configuration, and any required cache controls still apply. Source: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching

2.1

Shared context

Project instructions
User prompt
Skills
Domain glossary
Code and tests
Documentation

Agent

Context is the information available to the agent for a task. A new session needs some of the same background as a new teammate: what the app does, how the team works and which rules matter.

2.1 · Shared context

Static and dynamic context

Static context

Information supplied as a starting point, such as project instructions and tool definitions.

t1 t2 t3 t4
CLAUDE.md AGENTS.md skill descriptions tool definitions

Dynamic context

Information retrieved during a task, such as code, documentation and tool results.

t1 t2 t3 t4
skill instructions tool results project files subagent findings

Both use the context window: the information the model can consider at once.

2.1 · Shared context

Where static context comes from

  • System promptThe agent harness, or surrounding software, supplies instructions about the agent’s role and environment.
  • Tool definitionsDescriptions tell the agent what tools do and which inputs they accept.
  • User memorySaved preferences can apply across your projects.
  • Project memoryFiles such as AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md carry the team’s instructions.
  • Skill descriptionsShort descriptions help the agent choose a skill for the task.

Exactly what loads depends on the coding tool and your setup.

2.1 · Static context

What shared instructions help with

  • You don’t have to explain the same project rules in every conversation.
  • For example: “A report schedule defines when an export is due. A report run records what actually happened.”
  • Keeping that distinction in the project gives the next session a useful starting point.

2.1 · Static context

What would you leave out?

If the agent reads your project instructions on every task, what belongs there?

What would only be useful when it works on one specific feature?

2.1 · Static context

When shared instructions become a problem

  • Long instructions make the useful details harder to find.
  • Tokens are small pieces of text. Instructions use tokens too, so unrelated material can add time and cost.
  • An outdated rule can steer the agent toward the wrong behaviour.
  • Keep instructions current and check how the agent uses them.

2.1 · Static context

The code shows yesterday’s decision

http-wrapper

Old helper

  • Calls can wait indefinitely.
  • Each caller handles retries itself.
  • Failures are hard to follow across services.

Used in 27 places

response-wrapper

New helper

  • Timeouts and retries follow shared rules.
  • Authentication is handled in one place.
  • A shared trace ID makes calls easier to follow across services.

Used in 3 places

The team agreed to use the new helper, but nobody recorded that decision in the project.

Which example will the agent follow when it adds another call?

2.1 · Static context

A decision the next session can find

Without the written decision

×http-wrapper

Most existing code still uses the old helper.

With the written decision

AGENTS.mdUse response-wrapper for new calls. We are gradually replacing http-wrapper.
✓response-wrapper

The instruction explains why the new helper is the right choice.

We still need to check the result.

2.1 · Dynamic context

Dynamic context: finding what the task needs

Repository

Read the code and tests relevant to the task.

readsearch

Documentation

Check the details for the version in use.

Skills

SKILL.md

Subagents

separate session

2.1 · Dynamic context

What the project already tells it

  • Coding conventionsHow the team names and organises code.
  • Domain modelThe product’s concepts, rules and relationships.
  • Build and toolingBuild files explain how to run the app and its checks.
  • TestsExamples of what the code should do.
  • Git historyCommits and linked tickets can explain earlier decisions.

These are useful clues. They can also contain old patterns and mistakes.

2.1 · Dynamic context

MCP: connecting agents to tools

Model Context Protocol (MCP) is a standard way to connect an agent to tools. Each tool definition describes its purpose and the inputs it accepts.

{
"name": "create_issue",
"description": "Open a GitHub issue. Use when asked to file or track work.",what it is for
"inputSchema": {how to call it
"type": "object",
"properties": {
"repo": { "type": "string", "description": "owner/name" },
"title": { "type": "string" },
"body": { "type": "string" }
},
"required": ["repo", "title"]
}
}

The input schema describes the fields a tool accepts, such as a repository and title. Permissions determine what the agent can access.

2.1 · Dynamic context

Checking the documentation for your version

A suggestion to check

user = User.parse_obj(data)
return user.dict()

The suggested method may belong to an older library version.

context7 · get-library-docs →

After checking the documentation

user = User.model_validate(data)
return user.model_dump()

Use the method documented for the version in this project.

“Check how this version reads and validates user data. Show me the relevant documentation.”

2.1 · MCP

MCP permissions and prompt injection

Tool permissions

A connected tool may read information or change something outside the project. Check which permissions it has.

Prompt injection

Retrieved content can contain instructions that try to redirect the agent. Treat those instructions as untrusted input.

Least privilege

Give a tool only the access its task needs. Check who provides it and what it can change.

2.1 · Dynamic context

Skills: reusable instructions for a task

A skill is a saved set of instructions for a particular kind of task.

---
name: review-change
description: Compare a proposed change with its ticket
  and the project’s coding rules.

Description: helps select the skill

Review a change
1. Read the ticket and the project rules.
2. Check the behaviour against the examples.
3. Report findings with the relevant files.

Instructions: used for this task

1The agent may choose a skill from its description.
2You can ask for the skill by name.

Ask for a skill by name when you want to be sure which procedure the agent uses.

2.1 · Skills

Reading a skill before using it

The instructions

Does this procedure fit how your team works? Read it before using it.

The scripts and access

Check whether it can change files, publish something or contact an external service.

The description

Give each skill a clear purpose so the agent can tell when it applies.

2.1 · Skills

When a prompt is worth saving

You have used the same prompt several times, and it has helped.

  • The steps repeat across tasks.
  • You know what a useful result looks like.
  • You understand which instructions made the difference.
  • A teammate could use the same procedure.

Save the repeatable steps and say where someone still needs to decide.

2.1 · Skills

Using a skill someone else wrote

An existing skill can save you some writing and maintenance.

When it may help

  • It covers a tool your project uses.
  • The tool’s maintainers provide the instructions.
  • Someone keeps the procedure up to date.

What to check

  • Does it fit how your team works?
  • Is it current for your setup?
  • What can its scripts change or access?
  • Does it help with this particular task?

Read it first and check the results when you use it.

2.1 · Dynamic context

Subagents: a task in a separate context

  • A subagent is another agent assigned a specific task.
  • Give it the relevant context and the answer you need.
  • It works in its own context window.
  • Ask it to return findings and supporting file references.

Main agent

How to invoke a subagent

1
