2.1 · Subagents

Context isolation and orchestration

Context isolation

Read a large part of the project without crowding the main conversation.

A short answer

Bring back the findings and file references that matter for this task.

A fresh review

Review the change in another session with the ticket and project rules.

How the work can be shared

You → Orchestrator → Implementer Code reviewer Behaviour reviewer

An orchestrator coordinates the tasks and results while other agents work on specific parts.

The extra agent still takes time and costs money. Use one when the separate work is worth doing, and check its findings.

2.2

Intentionality and ambiguity

Before we ask for code, we need to make sure we mean the same thing.

2.2 · Intentionality

What you meant and what you asked for

What you mean

Export one report per schedule at 09:00 each day, using the schedule’s timezone.

You know the rule, but the agent has not seen it.

What you ask

“Add scheduled reports.”

The format, timing and retry behaviour are missing.

One possible guess

Export every report at 09:00 in the server’s timezone.

Each schedule needs its own timezone.

What you get

A working export that runs at the wrong time and creates duplicates.

Readable code can still describe the wrong product.

Write down the decisions that would make one answer right and another wrong.

2.2 · Intentionality

How much detail does this request need?

A short requestimportant rules are missingA detailed requestsome details may already be in the project

2.2 · Intentionality

A conversation before the code

What you type

“Before writing code, ask me about the parts of the scheduled report export that are still unclear. Ask one question at a time.”

What it asks back

01

Which data and format should the report include?

Agree the data range, file format and who can access it.

02

Which timezone determines when a report is due?

Agree what happens when clocks change.

03

What happens if processing runs late?

Agree how to handle missed runs without duplicate exports.

04

What happens if the schedule is disabled before processing?

Use examples to decide whether a pending run should still happen.

Keep the answers with the task so the next session can use them.

2.2 · Intentionality

Choosing how much help a task needs

Planning

Time for connected decisions

Choose a model that handles the task well.

Planning scheduled exports involves several connected decisions. Give those decisions enough time and use a model that handles the task well.

Implementing

A clearly described task

A faster model may be enough.

A small, clearly described implementation task may work well with a faster model.

Try both on representative tasks. Compare the result, the time spent and how much you had to correct.

2.2 · Intentionality

What we have agreed

Domain terminology

The domain glossary gives schedules, report runs and retries a shared meaning.

Acceptance criteria

These are the observable conditions the finished change must meet.

Invariants

These rules must remain true, such as a completed export remaining available after its schedule is disabled.

Write that agreement in the task or project documentation. Check it again when a decision changes.

2.3

Decomposition and boundaries

The report feature

Build and check

A working part

What is the first useful part of the report feature we can finish and check?

2.3 · Decomposition

What should we keep from the conversation?

Someone else needs to pick up this task tomorrow.

What would they need to know without reading the whole chat?

2.3 · Decomposition

What makes a useful specification?

A specification, or spec, records the agreed behaviour. Could another person use it to tell what should happen and whether the finished change does it?

2.3 · Decomposition

Vertical slices: a result we can build and check

A vertical slice delivers one usable behaviour through every layer it needs, so we can run and test it end to end.

Behavioural scope

A due schedule creates one downloadable report for that date.

Technical scope

Relevant code, existing rules and any work that must be ready first.

2.3 · Decomposition

What can we finish first?

Exports recur, retries can fail, and users need to see their run history.

Which of those behaviours could we build and check first? What would still be missing?

2.3 · Decomposition

User stories: the user’s side of the change

As a [person], I want [a capability], so that [a benefit].

  1. As a user, I want a report generated at an agreed time, so that I do not have to export it manually.
  2. As a user, I want report runs listed in my history, so that I can find completed exports.
  3. As a user, I want a warning before disabling a schedule, so that I understand what will stop.

These describe different pieces of work. The warning can be a later slice once scheduling works.

2.3 · Decomposition

Where would these changes go?

Which existing code knows about schedules? Which code creates an export? Which code shows the user their history?

Where should the due-date decision live so we do not repeat it in several places?

2.3 · Decomposition

Deep modules and interfaces

Specification

Schedules

Report exports

User screen

A deep module handles substantial behaviour behind a small interface: the operations callers use. The export module hides dates, retries and run tracking behind that interface. This is encapsulation.

2.3 · Decomposition

Why finish one behaviour at a time?

What becomes easier when each task ends with something we can run and check?

2.3 · Why it works

Focused context for each vertical slice

01

The first export task needs the scheduling rule, relevant code and a way to control the date in tests.

  • It does not need the whole discussion about report styling or warning wording.
  • A focused task gives the agent less unrelated material to work through.

2.3 · Why it works

A clear module boundary

02

If the scheduling rule lives in one place, the agent can find it and work on it there.

  • When the same decision appears in several parts of the app, it is easier to miss one or make them disagree.
  • Good organisation makes a change easier to understand and review.

2.3 · Decomposition

High coupling: one change touches everything

Coupling is how much parts of the code depend on each other. Here, the retry rule is spread across files that each know about dates, schedules and exports.

To change it safely, you have to understand how all those pieces work together. An agent faces the same problem. It may miss a connection or add another copy of the rule.

2.3 · Decomposition

Encapsulation keeps related decisions together

Gather the retry rules in one place. Other parts of the app ask for the result. Now a change to “retry a failed run once” has a clear home, and its tests can exercise that behaviour directly. There is less to read before making the next change.

2.3 · Why it works

Acceptance tests for each slice

03

Acceptance tests check the observable conditions from the ticket. Here, a due schedule should produce one report for that date.

  • Also check that it produces nothing early and cannot export the same scheduled run twice.
  • Those tests give the agent feedback and give the reviewer a concrete result to inspect.

2.3 · Decomposition

Where the specification lives

  • Keep the current feature description somewhere each session can find it, such as a linked ticket or the branch where you are working. A branch keeps this change separate from the shared version of the code. Update it when a decision changes.
  • Before removing temporary planning notes, preserve business rules and the reasons for important decisions in the project’s lasting documentation. Tests keep the expected behaviour checkable.

2.3 · Decomposition

A ticket a new session can pick up

spec.md → 01 02 03 04 05

02First scheduled export

1

Parent spec

Scheduled reports · feature rules

2

What to build

A due schedule creates one downloadable report for that date.

3

Acceptance criteria

  • No export before the due date.
  • One export for that scheduled date.
  • Repeated processing does not export it again.
  • The original report schedule stays unchanged.
4

Dependencies

01 · Schedule dates and timezones

  • 1Link to the agreed feature rules.
  • 2Describe the result someone can observe.
  • 3Acceptance criteria give examples that can become tests.
  • 4Name any work that must be ready first.

Another session should be able to begin from the ticket, without reading the whole chat.

2.3 · Decomposition

Dependencies and parallel work

  • Start with tasks whose prerequisites are ready. The agreed data shape lets the demo data work begin separately.
  • The export and date display need schedule details. Run history needs an agreed way to read results.

A dependency is work that must be ready first. Record it on the ticket before starting tasks in parallel.

2.3 · Architecture examples

Scattered decisions increase the reading cost

Illustrative design · scheduled reports

Scheduling rules appear in the controller, export worker and history screen.

A change to retry behaviour requires tracing all three paths. Each caller knows when a report is due and whether it has already run.

Where the change spreads

Dates, retries and completion tracking have several owners. A local fix can leave the other paths inconsistent.

Compare the dependencies needed for a specific change, rather than judging architecture by the number of files.

2.3 · Architecture examples

A small interface keeps decisions together

Illustrative design · scheduled reports

The scheduler asks one module to process a due report.

The export module owns due dates, duplicate protection and run history. Callers receive a result without repeating those rules.

A clear entry point

processDueReports(now)
→ run status and history

The boundary reduces what a caller must know. Its implementation and tests still need review.

2.3 · Architecture examples

Compare architecture by the change it supports

Understanding the change

Find the entry point, the rule owner, storage and the visible result.

For retry behaviour, follow one scheduled report from the trigger to the recorded result. Check where the decision is repeated.

Assessing the boundary

Look for clear interfaces, tests of the real rule and dependencies with a purpose. A tidy diagram alone is not evidence of correct code.

Treat diagrams as navigation aids. Confirm their claims in code, tests and the running application.

2.4

The context window

Context window filling 0%

Context management means choosing what enters the context window, what to retain and when to start a fresh session. The window has a token limit. Messages, instructions and tool results all use that space.

2.4 · The context window

Context rot: when useful details get lost

Quality of the work Tokens in the window →
  • Context rot describes declining reliability as context grows or becomes cluttered. Old errors and unrelated material can make useful details harder to use.
  • The agent may repeat a failed approach or overlook an earlier constraint. More material can also add time and cost, depending on the tool.
  • Watch for those signs. A full conversation is not something we need to aim for.

Illustration of a risk, not a measured curve. The effect depends on the model, task and information.

2.4 · The context window

Compaction: summarising the conversation

Earlier conversation

  • youadd the first scheduled export
  • readfeature rules
  • readExportService.java
  • editExportService.java
  • testduplicate export still fails
  • youeach schedule has its own timezone
  • editdue-date checks
  • testfirst export passes
→ compact

A shortened version

  • Task: first scheduled export
  • Each schedule has its own timezone
  • The first export works
  • Next: prevent duplicate exports

Some tools shorten the conversation into a summary. This is called compaction. It helps work continue, but can leave out a detail you still need.

2.4 · The context window

What compaction can lose

Original decisions

  • one export every day
  • each schedule has its own timezone
  • completed exports stay available
  • duplicate-export test needs work
  • disabled schedules do not run
  • schedule settings remain unchanged
→

One possible summary

  • one export every day
  • each schedule has its own timezone
  • completed exports stay available
  • duplicate-export test needs work
  • disabled schedules do not run
  • schedule settings remain unchanged
→

A later summary

  • one export every day
  • each schedule has its own timezone
  • completed exports stay available
  • duplicate-export test needs work
  • disabled schedules do not run
  • schedule settings remain unchanged
  • The summary might keep “daily report exports” and lose “each schedule has its own timezone.”
  • That small omission changes the feature.

Keep important rules and rejected approaches on the ticket. After a summary, check that the next proposed step still fits them.

2.4 · The context window

Context management between sessions

  • Save the workKeep the current working version before ending the session.
  • Write a handoverRecord what is done, what comes next and what did not work.
  • Start another sessionContinue from the ticket and branch with the relevant background.

This is especially useful when you are starting another task or the old conversation contains several abandoned approaches.

2.5

Execution and implementation

Test-driven development (TDD) follows red, green, refactor: write a failing test, make it pass, then improve the code while keeping the tests green.

2.5 · Implementation

Giving the agent a feedback loop

You run each check

it writes the code → you run it → you read the error → you explain it → it tries again

If you have to run every command and explain every failure, the agent has to wait for you at each step.

The agent can run the checks

it writes the code → it runs it → it reads the error → it tries again

When it can run the tests and read the results, it can fix many mistakes itself.

Give it the commands and access it needs for those checks. You still decide what the checks should prove.

2.5 · Implementation

Acceptance criteria as executable tests

Example test: scheduled date

@Test
void dueScheduleExportsOnce() {
  var schedule = dailyAt("09:00", "UTC");
  setTime("2027-01-10T09:00:00Z");

  processDueReports();
  processDueReports();

  assertThat(exportsFor(schedule)).hasSize(1);
}
  • Create a daily schedule due at 09:00 UTC. Set the test clock to that time and process it twice.
  • The test should find exactly one export, even though processing ran twice.

Read the test before asking for the implementation. Does this example express what we agreed?

2.5 · Implementation

Mocks and stubs: what did this test run?

This test only calls a mock

@Test
void dueScheduleExportsOnce() {
  var exports = mock(ExportService.class);
  when(exports.countFor(schedule))
    .thenReturn(1);

  assertThat(exports.countFor(schedule))
    .isEqualTo(1);
}
  • A mock replaces the real export service. The stub returns a count of one. The test then checks that prepared response.
  • It passes, but it never runs the scheduling rule.

Check what each test actually calls. Could it pass even if scheduled processing were missing?

2.5 · Implementation

Mutation testing: checking the tests

Temporarily remove the report export

// ExportService: deliberate test mutation
if (dueOn(schedule, today)) {
  exportReport(schedule);
}

$ ./gradlew test

All tests still pass

The missing export should have made its test fail.

  • Temporarily remove the export and run its test.
  • The test should fail. If it still passes, find out what it is really checking.

Restore the code and confirm that the test passes again. Do this in an isolated working copy so you can safely discard the deliberate mistake.

2.5 · Implementation

Observability: logs explain the run

Logs from the running app

  • job: scheduled reports
  • schedule: 8811
  • format: CSV; timezone: UTC
  • created: 1 January 2027
  • due: 10 January 2027
  • processing date: 9 January 2027
  • decision: not due yet
  • exports created: 0
  • next due date: 10 January 2027
  • Useful output might say:
  • “Schedule 8811. Due: 10 January. Processing date: 9 January. Export skipped because the schedule is not due yet.”
  • That gives the agent something specific to investigate. A message such as “export failed” does not.

Observability means understanding the running system from its outputs. Log the relevant decisions without exposing private user information.

2.5 · Implementation

Browser automation and visual checks

localhost:5173/reports
Export ↑ the button covers the status

Automated tests pass

  • The tests pass, but the export button covers the report status.
  • Browser automation can follow a flow and capture the screen. End-to-end tests check that the connected parts work together.

Check the screens and states affected by the change, including a narrow screen where the layout may behave differently.

2.5 · Implementation

What the agent needs before it starts

  • Run the appThe command and setup the agent needs.
  • Run the testsWhich checks to run and what they should prove.
  • Inspect the resultLogs for failures and browser access for screens.
  • Know when it is doneThe ticket’s acceptance criteria: observable conditions for completion.

Keep this information where the next session can find it too.

2.5 · Implementation

When an attempt gets stuck

  • Commit a checkpointA Git commit records a working checkpoint you can return to.
  • Pause and inspectIf the agent keeps repeating an unsuccessful approach, pause and inspect what went wrong. Clarify the ticket if a requirement was missing.
  • Choose the next attemptPreserve useful work before undoing the failed attempt. Then continue with a smaller task or a fresh session.

2.5 · Worked example

An orchestrator, implementer and reviewers

Each handover records the work and findings. Passing checks and agent reviews support the final human review.

2.5 · Prototyping

What if we need to see the idea first?

We want to warn users before disabling a recurring report schedule.

Where should that warning appear, and will people understand it?

Could a small demo help us decide before we build the full feature?

2.5 · Prototyping

A throwaway prototype to answer one question

  • The questionWhere should the disable warning appear, and is it clear?
  • The prototypeUse fake schedules and try two versions of the warning.
  • The next stepRecord the decision and keep this temporary demo separate from production code.

Exploratory “vibe coding” can help try an idea quickly. Treat this prototype as an experiment and record what you learned before building the lasting feature.

2.6

Validation and review

After implementation, a critic subagent reviews architecture, UX and tests. Deterministic checks establish specific facts. A human uses that evidence to review the change strategically.

2.6 · Review

A fresh critic reviews the implementation

Give the critic the spec, acceptance criteria, base and current commits, project rules and commands to run the app and checks.

  • ArchitectureInspect the changed modules and their callers. Check encapsulation, interfaces and the project’s engineering practices.
  • User experienceRun the app. Try realistic journeys and inspect screenshots.
  • TestsRead assertions against the acceptance criteria. Check that real behaviour runs and meaningful mistakes make tests fail.

Return findings with evidence and unresolved questions. A fresh context helps, but the critic can still miss things.

2.6 · Review

Judgment, validation and enforcement

  • Model-driven guidance“This module exposes too much.” The critic reasons about architecture, UX and test quality. Investigate its findings.
  • Deterministic validation“This fixture produced one export after two runs.” Explicit rules produce checkable results under controlled conditions.
  • Platform enforcement“Merge blocked: required check failed.” The platform applies configured rules independently of the critic’s opinion.

A passing check establishes only what it checks. A model’s confident review is not proof that a policy was enforced.

2.6 · Review

Architecture review beyond coding style

The critic reads the change in the wider codebase. Does it preserve useful boundaries and keep related rules together?

Encapsulation

Keep due-date and retry details behind a small interface.

Module boundaries

Look for duplicated scheduling rules and dependencies crossing the wrong boundary.

Interfaces

Check what callers must know. Avoid exposing internal state just for this change.

Engineering practices

Check cohesion, unnecessary abstraction and how easily the rule can be tested.

Failure handling

Inspect retries, duplicate processing and partial failures across modules.

Existing conventions

Check naming, error handling and reuse of the project’s established patterns.

Report the affected files and callers, the consequence and a suggested direction. A linter can enforce a dependency rule; good encapsulation still needs judgment.

2.6 · Review

UX review needs the running application

What the code shows

<div className="warning">
  <h4>Before you disable</h4>
  <p>{warning.message}</p>
</div>

/* warning.css */
.warning p {
  display: -webkit-box;
  -webkit-line-clamp: 2;
  overflow: hidden;
}
  • ✓StandardsUses the existing warning component.
  • ✓Text checkThe warning text is present.

What the user sees

Before you disable

Disabling this schedule stops all future report exports. Completed reports remain available in your history, but the pending export for 10 January will not run.

The text cuts off before the user can read the explanation.

The critic follows the disable-schedule journey in the app, reproduces the clipped warning and attaches a screenshot. Reading the diff alone can miss this.

2.6 · Review

Browser assertions and UX judgment

  • Short text

    Example checked

  • Long warning

    Still to check

  • No export due

    Still to check

  • Narrow screen

    Still to check

  • Slow response

    Still to check

  • Scripted check: this fixture shows “future exports will stop” before confirmation. Record the assertion and its result.
  • Critic judgment: is the warning readable and clear? Try these states in the app and inspect screenshots.

Automating a browser does not make every conclusion deterministic. Record steps, test data, screenshots and states not tried so a human can assess the UX finding.

2.6 · Review

The critic checks the tests against the spec

The change to the test

// ExportServiceTest.java
  var schedule = dueOn("2027-01-10");

- setDate("2027-01-10");
+ setDate("2027-01-11");
  processDueReports();
  assertThat(exportsFor(schedule)).hasSize(1);
  • ✓Code styleThe code follows the project style.
  • ✓Test runThe edited test passes.
  • ✗RequirementIt now checks the day after the scheduled date.

The original requirement

TASK-112 · First scheduled export

A due schedule creates one report on its scheduled date.

The implementation exports late. Changing the expected date does not fix it.

The critic compares changed assertions with the acceptance criteria. Here, the test passes because someone moved the expected date. The functional requirement still fails.

2.6 · Review

Do the tests catch meaningful mistakes?

Review requestCritic: map each acceptance criterion to a test and inspect what it calls. In an isolated copy, introduce one mistake at a time, run the relevant test and restore the change. Report gaps and missed mutations.

RequirementTestDeliberate mistakeResult
One export per scheduled date scheduledExportRunsOnce allow a second export CAUGHT
No early export noExportBeforeDueDate export one day early CAUGHT
Completed exports stay available exportsSurviveDisable delete an earlier export MISSED
Disabled schedules do not run No test found Not checked NO TEST

Choosing useful mutations takes judgment. Running the tests shows which assertions detect each specific mutation.

Include test references and command results. Review fixtures and mocks too: a passing test must exercise the real rule. Keep the critic’s review separate from implementation fixes.

2.6 · Review

Deterministic checks establish technical facts

Build and types

Does this revision compile and satisfy the configured type checks?

Acceptance and regression

With a fixed date and data, do the stated assertions pass?

Mutation results

Which selected mutations caused a test to fail?

Lint and dependency rules

Does the code violate a configured style or module-dependency rule?

Secrets and dependencies

Do the configured scanners flag a secret or disallowed dependency?

Schema and migrations

Does the migration run on the test database and meet the stated constraints?

Record the revision, commands, inputs and tool or ruleset versions. Flaky tests and changing data weaken repeatability. A green pipeline does not establish overall compliance.

2.6 · Review

Human review: spend attention strategically

  • Read access rules, irreversible actions and uncertain behaviour closely. Check both the implementation and the evidence against the acceptance criteria.
  • Routine formatting usually needs less attention when checks cover it. A small wording change can still matter if it changes a user’s decision.

Use the critic’s findings to guide attention, then inspect high-risk areas it did not flag. The absence of a finding is not a reason to skip them.

2.6 · Review

Build the mental model by behaviour

Git diff: files

  • SchedulesService.java+14 −3
  • ReportController.java+9 −1
  • ReportResponse.java+6 −0
  • DemoData.java+58 −4
  • Schedule.java+11 −2
  • ReportRun.java+27 −1
  • ExportService.java+94 −18
  • ExportResult.java+8 −0
  • RunHistoryService.java+46 −7
  • HistoryController.java+12 −3
  • and 13 more files

Git diff groups changes by file. Related behaviour can be scattered across that list.

→ critic groups the change

Review map: behaviours

  • 1 Report due datescheck the rule SchedulesService · ExportService · date tests
  • 2 Recording exportscheck the result ReportRun · RunHistoryService · duplicate tests
  • 3 Showing the resulttry the screen HistoryController · HistoryView · screen evidence

For each group, link the requirement, code, tests and visible result. Explain the connections between groups.

Keep related changes contextually close in the review, even across files. Follow one behaviour end to end to build and retain a mental model, then check the map against the actual diff.

2.6 · Review

What the critic hands to the human

  • A map of the changeGroup linked files and tests by behaviour. Show which acceptance criteria each group addresses.
  • Findings with evidenceFor each architecture, UX or test issue: consequence, file references or reproduction steps, and supporting results.
  • Known limitsList untested states, missing checks, assumptions and unresolved decisions. Separate observed failures from concerns.
  • Review prioritiesExplain what deserves a close read and why. Attach screenshots, check results and the exact revision reviewed.

The human uses this package to navigate the code and validate the functional criteria. The summary supports the review; it does not replace it.

2.6 · Review

Where the checks fit in the review loop

  • During implementationRun fast deterministic checks as the code changes. They give the implementer immediate feedback.
  • Post-implementationA fresh critic reviews architecture, UX and tests, runs relevant checks and prepares evidence for the human.
  • Human reviewRead by behaviour and consequence. Resolve findings, assess functional criteria and make the acceptance decision.
  • Before mergingRequired CI checks and platform approvals apply to the proposed revision. Recheck affected evidence after fixes.

Keep findings, check results and approvals tied to the code reviewed. A fix can change what needs to be tested or reviewed again.

2.6 · Review

The human owns the acceptance decision

Evidence to work with

  • Critic findings on architecture, UX and tests
  • Deterministic check results and their scope
  • A review map linking behaviour across files
  • Untested states and unresolved questions

Decisions to make

  • Does it meet the functional criteria?
  • Does the architecture fit the wider codebase?
  • Can users understand and use it?
  • Are remaining risks acceptable under our policies?

The critic recommends, checks validate specific facts, and the human decides. Module 3 carries these review habits into CI when the feature becomes a pull request.

2.7

Iteration and termination

A run needs termination conditions: completion, a turn or budget limit, or a decision that needs a person. Each session should leave a handover for the next one.

2.7 · Iteration

What will the next session know?

What this session found

  • Where the scheduling rule lives
  • Why the first approach failed
  • Which terms the team agreed on
  • Which unrelated test was already failing
× session
ends

What the next session can find

What we saved

Save the information needed to continue in a place the next session will read. Do not assume the conversation will carry over.

2.7 · Iteration

The code and the ticket

The branch

The branch holds the work completed so far.

scheduled-reports First scheduled export works

The ticket

The ticket explains what remains, why it matters and which approaches already failed. Put the handover there too.

Use the team’s issue tracker.

#42 Late processing Decision needed on missed runs

A new session can read both. It should not need someone to reconstruct the previous conversation.

2.7 · Iteration

Git worktrees: separate working copies

git worktree add ../report-history -b report-history

  • Git worktrees let several agents use separate working folders and branches from the same repository.
  • One can work on report exports while another works on the history display, once their shared details are agreed.

Their edits stay in separate folders. You still need to bring the changes together and check that they work together.

2.7 · Iteration

Worktrees and execution isolation

Separate working copies

  • ✓Working files
  • ✓Branch and index (staging area)
  • ✓Edits not yet saved in Git

Resources that may still be shared

  • •A database on port 5432
  • •A server on port 8080
  • •Caches, temporary files and settings

Worktrees separate files. A sandbox isolates execution with controlled resources and access. Check whether databases, ports and caches are still shared.

2.7 · Iteration

The issue tracker as shared memory

#42

Late processing and missed runs

Completed exports remain available. Repeated processing must not create duplicate runs.

Latest progress note

Scheduled exports work. We still need a rule for missed runs after an outage. Server time loses each schedule’s timezone.

branch: late-processing

  • The ticket says what the change should do.
  • The latest note explains what works and what is unresolved.
  • A new session can see the rejected approach and its reason.

That record lets the next person continue without reconstructing the conversation.

2.7 · Iteration

Integrating changes through pull requests

  • Each task returns as a small pull request: a proposed code change that someone can review before it joins the shared work.
  • In this example, the tasks merge into a shared feature branch. After each merge, update the remaining branches and run the checks again.

The complete feature then goes through the final review before reaching the main branch. Other teams may organise their branches differently.

2.7 · Iteration

More agents also means more work to review

4 agents in separate worktrees
→
4 changes ready at the same time
→
1 reviewer time needed for each

If one person must review all four changes, a queue forms. Start with the amount of work the team can check carefully.

2.7 · Termination

What should happen when the agent gets stuck?

It has made several attempts, but the task still does not meet the requirements.

When should it stop, and what should it leave for you?

2.7 · Termination

Termination with a useful handover

#42 · comment

Stopped at turn 14

  • Met Scheduled exports work, including duplicate protection.
  • Not met Late processing treatment remains unresolved.
  • Tried A shared server clock loses each schedule’s timezone.
  • Blocked on Should an outage trigger every missed run or only the latest?

For the product decision

Agree the missing rule using a worked example.

For the next session

Read the decision and continue from the working version.

The next person can see what works, what remains and why the work stopped.

2.7 · Termination

Before a run continues without you

  • TriggerThe request, schedule or event that starts the task.
  • Checkable goalThe acceptance criteria the available checks should judge.
  • EvaluatorThe check that decides whether the goal is met or more work is needed.
  • Termination conditionsStop at completion, a turn or budget limit, or a decision that needs you.

When a run stops, it should record the completed work and what remains.

2.8

Framework comparison

We have seen how written requirements, repeated checks and separate reviewers fit together. These approaches organise those ideas in different ways.

2.8 · Spec-driven

Spec-driven development

Write it down

The specification

Agree on the expected behaviour and keep it with the project.

→
Derive from it

Tasks and implementation

Use the description to guide the work and its tests.

→
Check against it

Review against the rules

Check whether the result matches what was agreed.

This is often called spec-driven development. Keep the written requirements current when a decision changes.

2.8 · Loop

The agent loop: trigger, work, evaluate

Starts

Trigger

A request, schedule or event starts the task.

→
Works

Agent turn

The agent reads the task, makes changes and runs checks.

→
Checks

Evaluator

Decide whether the goal is met or another round is needed.

Continue until the goal is met, a limit is reached or a decision needs a person.

An automated loop is useful when its checks can recognise the result we want.

2.8 · Roles

Role-based workflows

Decides

Architect

Agree on the change and record the decisions.

→
Builds

Implementer

Work through a clearly described task in another session.

→
Checks

Reviewer

Check the result against the task and the project rules.

This is often called role-based development. Each handover needs a clear record. The job title alone does not establish the quality of the work.

2.8 · The throughline

What does this way of working actually check?

Look at any proposed workflow and find the checks.

What mistakes can they catch? What happens when they fail? Which decisions still come back to a person?

Next, we connect this same loop to local hooks and CI: automatic feedback while coding, then a fresh review when the feature becomes a pull request.

Module 3 · Hooks and CI

The delivery loop keeps going

Follow the feature through local checks and shared review.

01 / 08

3 · Agenda

What we’ll cover in Module 3

  • HooksAgent and Git hooks: when they run and how they give feedback during coding.
  • Agents in CIHow a PR starts shared checks and a fresh reviewer with the right context.
  • Review walkthroughWalk through illustrative review findings, verify the evidence and inspect coverage.
  • Close the loopHow findings lead to another coding iteration and a human decision to merge.

We’ll connect the delivery practices from Module 2 to local checks and CI.

3 · Connecting the delivery practices

How Module 2 connects to CI

  • Agreed behaviourThe interview and spec explain the intended feature behaviour, including its edge cases. 2.2–2.3
  • Reviewed ticketsEach ticket has code, tests and review findings. Completed tickets join the feature branch. 2.5–2.7
  • A usable handoffThe ticket records and readable diff let another agent or a human understand the change. 2.4 / 2.7

Next: connect this work to automatic feedback while coding and when the feature becomes a PR.

3 · Hooks

Hooks connect events to actions

When this happens, run this.

  • EventA session starts, a file is edited or a commit is attempted.
  • ActionThe tool runs a configured command: supply context, format code or run a check.
  • ResultThe hook can provide feedback; supported hooks can also block an action.

The tool triggers the action. The check determines its result. A model-based check still involves judgment.

3 · Agent hooks

Hooks inside the coding session

  • Session startsSupply the current branch and ticket reference so the agent can pick up the handoff. Context · 2.4
  • After an editFormat the changed file or run a small, relevant check. Feedback · 2.5
  • Before a tool callCheck the proposed action and reject operations outside the configured boundaries. Autonomy · 2.7

Agent hooks belong to the tool running the session. Available events and blocking behaviour depend on that tool.

3 · Git hooks

Git hooks check work before a commit

Example · executable .git/hooks/pre-commit

#!/bin/sh
set -e
cd frontend
npx tsc -b
  • Git triggers this hookIt runs when a human or an agent attempts a commit.
  • A failing check stops the commitThe command returns an error and Git leaves the changes uncommitted.
  • Choose checks that fit the momentKeep frequent checks quick. Local hooks can be bypassed, so shared validation still matters.

Agent hooks follow the agent’s lifecycle. Git hooks follow Git operations. Both can call the same project checks.

3 · The local feedback loop

A failed check feeds the coding agent

Illustrative sequence · a web frontend

Agent attempts a commit
→ pre-commit runs typechecking

Type 'string' is not assignable
to type 'number'.

Commit stopped. Changes remain local.
  • Read the failureThe coding agent sees the command’s output and locates the mismatch.
  • Correct the implementationIt fixes the value or its use, keeping the intended behaviour intact.
  • Run the check againThe next commit attempt runs the hook again. Passing allows the commit.

This is the 2.5 loop with an automatic trigger: edit → check → feedback → correction.

3 · The shared handoff

The feature becomes a pull request

Reviewed ticket branches → feature/scheduled-reports → PR to main

  • Assemble the featureRepeat the ticket loop from 2.7 and check the integrated result. The walkthrough follows an integrated feature.
  • Publish the handoffInclude the spec, ticket references, check results and readable review summary.
  • Review a revisionThe PR identifies the proposed changes. New commits need current evidence.

The coding conversation can end. The repository carries what the next reviewer needs.

3 · Agents in CI

CI starts checks and a fresh reviewer

  • PR opened or updatedA repository event starts the configured workflows.
  • Checks runBuild, typechecking and tests can validate the proposed revision in CI.
  • An agent reviewsA separate job starts a fresh reviewer with the changes, available context and review instructions.
  • Results return to the PRCheck results and review findings become the next inputs to the delivery loop.

CI means continuous integration. It can run both project checks and an AI reviewer. The walkthrough focuses on the reviewer job.

3 · Checks and judgment

Tests and AI review contribute different evidence

A test checks a stated rule

Process the same due schedule twice.

Expected: one report export for that scheduled date.

A passing assertion supports this behaviour for the tested inputs.

A reviewer questions an edge case

A schedule is due, then the user disables it before processing.

Should the pending run still happen?

Check that interpretation against the agreement from 2.2.

An AI finding needs evidence and assessment. A successful reviewer job means the job ran; its conclusions still need checking.

3 · Context for the CI agent

The reviewer needs the Module 2 handoff

  • Scope · 2.3 / 2.7Give it the PR’s base and head revisions. It is reviewing the assembled feature across tickets.
  • Intent · 2.2 / 2.3Supply the agreed behaviour, spec and acceptance criteria. Check that the reviewer actually receives them.
  • Review brief · 2.6Check standards and requirements. Ask for a triggering scenario, affected code, impact and evidence.

The context lesson from 2.4 still applies: a large diff can exceed the input budget. Inspect excluded files and verification gaps.

3 · An illustrative reviewer setup

How a PR-Agent job can work

  • Trigger.github/workflows/pr-agent.yml starts the review on eligible PR events or a supported review command.
  • Context and instructionsPR-Agent reads changes through the GitHub API. .pr_agent.toml adds review guidance; the configured model evaluates the input.
  • FeedbackIt posts a summary and review findings on the PR. In this illustrative setup, the job cannot push code and does not approve or merge.

This example reviews code. UI/UX review from 2.6 would need a separate job with a running app, test data and browser access.

3 · Review walkthrough

Follow the feature into its PR

A pull request carries the feature diff, check results and the reviewer’s findings.

The reviewer’s findings are compared with the code and the agreed behaviour.

False positives and excluded files show why a completed review job still needs assessment.

OutcomeThe review habits from 2.6 help decide what deserves a fix, clarification or dismissal.

3 · Reading the review

Assess the finding before asking for a fix

Business question · Late processing

Disabling a due schedule before processing may change whether its pending export runs.

Confirm the intended rule and its test coverage. An unresolved product decision is not automatically a defect.

False positive · Already handled

An illustrative finding says the disabled state is ignored. The proposed revision already checks it:

if (!schedule.enabled()) {
  return SKIPPED;
}

Check the proposed fix against the actual revision.

Record whether each finding needs a fix, a clarified decision or dismissal, with the evidence behind that choice.

3 · Return to the 2.7 loop

Feed confirmed work back to the coding agent

  • Give it a precise taskRecord the confirmed finding in a ticket: the scenario, intended behaviour, affected revision and evidence.
  • Implement and checkUse the ticket branch and worktree workflow from 2.7. Add a regression test where appropriate and review the correction.
  • Update the feature PRMerge the completed correction into the feature branch and push. Configured checks and PR review run on the update.

The reviewer supplies feedback. The implementing agent makes the change. Repeat affected checks and reviews; record unresolved blockers.

3 · Human acceptance

A merge needs current evidence

  • ChecksRequired builds and tests pass for the revision being accepted.
  • Review findingsConfirmed problems are resolved. Dismissed findings and remaining gaps have an explanation.
  • Human decisionUse the readable diff from 2.7 and evidence for the complete user journey to assess the feature.
  • Platform rulesBranch rules can require checks and approvals before merge. Enforcement depends on configuration and bypass rights.

Keep the review outcome separate from the green status of the job that produced it.

Modules 2 & 3 · One delivery loop

One feature, one continuing feedback loop

Module 2: agree the feature, slice it, implement it and review it.

Local hooks: trigger checks while the coding agent can act on the result.

CI: run shared checks and a fresh review when the PR changes.

Continue: assess findings, correct the code and gather evidence for human acceptance.

Modules 2 & 3 · Bringing it together

A feature starts as an idea

The intent is there. The boundaries and behaviour are still fuzzy.

Modules 2 & 3 · The delivery loop Click or → to continue · ← to go back

Module 4 · Harness engineering

Harness engineering

How do you take a working capability and make it available to an agent?

60 minutes · one exercise, then the discussion

You will be able to Take a capability that already works, and make it available to an agent.

0:00 Last slot of the day. The room has been running agents since 09:15 and is tired. Do not open with theory. Open by saying what they are going to have working in thirty minutes, then get them into it.

Budget: 9 min on retrieval (2 on RAG, 2 on what is in the table, 2 on semantic search, 3 on keyword versus semantic), 2 min briefing the exercise, ~30 min hands-on, then 4 on the scope question, 3 + 3 on the two doors, 5 on the trade-offs, 3 on the broken skill, 1 to close. That is 60, with no slack. If you start late, compress the three retrieval slides after RAG to a minute each rather than touching the debrief. Everything after the hands-on is the conclusion, and together it is about 20 minutes that must not be squeezed.

If the hands-on overruns, take it out of the two solution slides, not the discussion. People who built the thing do not need it explained back to them at length; people who did not finish need the comparison more than the walkthrough.

Open: the objective on this slide no longer matches the SoW, which still says “extend and orchestrate agents with tools, memory and subagents and reason about what a workflow costs.” Subagents and cost were cut from this module. Sophie needs to know before KBC notices.

Connects toEverything about what the always-loaded layer costs was already said in 2.4. Do not re-teach it. This module is about distribution and ownership: what you host, what you hand over, and who holds the keys.

4 · RAG

RAG, quickly

The model has never seen your documents. So you search first, and put what you found in the prompt.

~2 min. This and the three slides after it are the only teaching before they build. Keep this one at this altitude; the next three open up the table and the search box. Nobody in this room is going to write a retrieval pipeline today, and 2.1 of Dataroots' Agentic AI Academy is where that lives if they want it.

The two things that have to land: the passages and their embeddings are loaded once and ahead of time, so search at question time is a single SQL query; and the model still only sees what you put in the prompt, so retrieval is about choosing what to paste, nothing more mysterious than that.

The one thing that is not precomputed is the question itself. Hybrid embeds the question at run time, which is one call out to Azure OpenAI before the query runs. Worth a sentence, because it is the piece that fails first if the network is unhappy, and they will see it if it does.

Why hybrid: read the caption and leave it there. The third slide from here takes it apart.

If someone asks about embeddings, the slide after next is the answer, so say so and click on.

Say what the corpus is before the next slide, or the exercise brief will not make sense: two public-domain books about beer, The Curiosities of Ale & Beer and Beer: Its History and Its Economic Value, chopped into 663 passages and already loaded into a Postgres database the VMs can reach. The tool is on their VM, the data is not.

Say why it is beer and not the codebase, because someone will ask in the first minute. Two reasons, both worth thirty seconds: the model has demonstrably never memorised these books, so a right answer can only have come from retrieval; and a corpus nobody has an opinion about keeps the hour on the harness instead of on the content. The mechanics are identical the day it is your runbooks in that table.

Connects to2.1 of Dataroots' Agentic AI Academy is where this pipeline was built by hand. Say that the loading is already done here on purpose: today is about the door in front of it, not the chunking behind it.

4 · RAG

What is in the database

One table, chunks. Each row holds a passage, the book it came from, and its embedding.

sourcecontent · about 400 words, excerptembedding
The Curiosities of Ale & Beer…the duty on malt from July 5th, 1785, to the same day 1786, produced a million and a half of money to the support of the State…[ 1,536 numbers ]
Beer: Its History and Its Economic Value…every brewer had to pay duty, so that the king might not be defrauded, was obliged to give notice of every brewing to a commissioner…[ 1,536 numbers ]
Beer: Its History and Its Economic Value…A beer tax also was levied on vassals who brewed their own beer…[ 1,536 numbers ]
schema, abridged 
CREATE TABLE chunks (
  id        SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  source    TEXT,
  content   TEXT,
  embedding vector(1536)
);
-- keyword search reads this
CREATE INDEX ON chunks USING GIN (to_tsvector('english', content));
-- semantic search reads this
CREATE INDEX ON chunks USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops);
  • 663 rows. 466 from The Curiosities of Ale & Beer, 197 from Beer: Its History and Its Economic Value.
  • Cut by word count, not by meaning. Each passage is 400 words and overlaps its neighbour by 50, so a sentence cut at one edge is whole in the next.
  • Two indexes, one per search. The text index serves keyword search; the vector index serves semantic search. The next two slides use both.

~2 min. Three clicks, one per bullet. The point of the slide is that there is nothing hidden: a table with four columns, and two indexes. Everything the exercise does is a query against it.

The rows are real. All three excerpts are from the loaded corpus, lab/module-4/assets/beer_books.jsonl, trimmed to a sentence. They are all about tax, on purpose: the next two slides search for “how was beer taxed?”. The embedding column is shown as a count rather than values because nobody can read 1,536 numbers, and anything we printed would be made up.

Passages start and end mid-sentence. Say so before someone runs the jar and asks why the result begins halfway through a thought. The chunking counts words and ignores sentences and chapters. The 50-word overlap is the cheap fix: two of the history book's passages share the sentence about every brewer paying duty for exactly that reason. Better chunking exists; it was not the point of today.

The indexes are what make search fast, and they map one to one onto the next two slides. GIN over the stemmed words is keyword search; HNSW over the vectors with cosine distance is semantic search. Without them both still work, they just read every row.

The schema is abridged. The real one in lab/module-4/pipeline/prepare_dataset.py names the indexes and adds IF NOT EXISTS; nothing else differs.

Connects toThe “built once” row on the previous slide is this table being filled. The two indexes are the two searches on the next two slides, and the exercise SQL queries this table directly.

4 · RAG

Semantic search: closeness of meaning

An embedding model turns a piece of text into a vector. Text that means similar things points in a similar direction.

~2 min. Two clicks: what gets stored, then how close is close. Start on the picture alone and say the one sentence that matters: similar meaning, similar direction, and the angle between two arrows is the distance between two ideas.

Point at the duty passage. It shares no words with the question and it is still the closest thing in the picture. That is the capability keyword search does not have, and it is why the next slide exists.

The numbers are illustrative. The shape is right: related text scores well above unrelated text. Do not quote 0.71 as measured. The 1,536 is real: the lab asks text-embedding-3-large for 1,536 dimensions, half its full 3,072, and the column is vector(1536).

The last line is the SQL from the exercise brief. Say that out loud so the brief on the slide after next is not a wall of unfamiliar syntax: <=> is pgvector's cosine distance, and ordering by it is the whole of semantic search.

If someone asks why cosine and not straight-line distance: direction carries the meaning, length mostly does not, and the OpenAI embeddings are normalised to length one anyway, so the two give the same order. One sentence, then move on.

Connects toThe question vector is the run-time embedding call from the RAG slide, the one that needs Azure OpenAI to be reachable. The next slide puts this search next to keyword search and fuses the two.

4 · RAG

Keyword, semantic, then both

Each search finds passages the other misses. Hybrid runs both and fuses the rankings.

~3 min. Four clicks: keyword, semantic, fusion, then what happens to the result. Leave the question on screen alone for a beat first and ask the room which passages they would expect to come back.

Keyword search is Postgres full-text search. It stems the question, so taxed matches tax and taxes, and then it needs the word to be there. Precise and literal: it never finds the duty passage, however relevant. It is also what you want for exact names, dates, part numbers and error codes, where a near miss in meaning is a wrong answer.

Semantic search is the previous slide. It finds the duty passage first, with no shared word at all. Its weakness is the mirror image: a query for a specific act or year can come back with passages that are about the same topic and name a different one. It also always returns its nearest neighbours, so it hands you something even when nothing in the corpus is relevant.

Fusion only uses rank, never the raw scores. That matters, because a keyword score and a cosine similarity are on different scales and cannot be added. Reciprocal rank fusion gives each passage 1/(60 + its rank) from each list it appears in and adds them up. The scores on the slide are worked out that way: tax on malt is 1/61 + 1/62, so being found by both beats being first in one. The 60 is the conventional constant; it stops the very top rank from dominating. The SQL in the exercise brief does exactly this, in its rrf step, over the top 50 of each list.

The last row is what happens after. The top five come back with the book each passage came from, they go into the prompt next to the question, and the model writes from them. Keep it at that. Who does the writing, the tool or the agent that called it, is the question on the “How much should the tool do?” slide after the exercise, and it lands better if the room has not been told.

The passages on this slide are labels, not quotes. They stand for the kind of passage each search returns. If someone wants to see the real ones, run the jar with the same question during the exercise.

Connects toThe exercise brief on the next slide, whose SQL is these three boxes in one query. Back to 2.1 for why what goes into the window is the whole game.

4 · Exercise

Make the search reachable

This already searches the books and prints what it found. It runs in your terminal, where the agent cannot see it.

already done 
// one query: keywords and vector, fused by rank
String HYBRID_SQL = """
WITH semantic AS (SELECT id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY
    embedding <=> ?::vector, id) AS rank_v FROM chunks
  ORDER BY embedding <=> ?::vector, id LIMIT 50),
keyword AS (SELECT id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY
    ts_rank(to_tsvector('english', content),
      plainto_tsquery('english', ?)) DESC, id) AS rank_k
  FROM chunks WHERE to_tsvector('english', content)
    @@ plainto_tsquery('english', ?) LIMIT 50),
rrf AS (SELECT COALESCE(s.id, k.id) AS id,
    COALESCE(1.0/(60+s.rank_v),0)
      + COALESCE(1.0/(60+k.rank_k),0) AS score
  FROM semantic s FULL OUTER JOIN keyword k ON s.id = k.id)
SELECT c.id, c.source, c.content, rrf.score
FROM rrf JOIN chunks c ON c.id = rrf.id
ORDER BY rrf.score DESC, c.id LIMIT 5""";
  • Already done. A Postgres instance loaded with the chunks and pgvector enabled, and an Azure Foundry instance with keys for the model and the embedder.
  • What we want. That same capability, available inside the agent.
  • 30 minutes. There is more than one way to do this.
.env.example 
PG_URL=postgresql://bookadmin:<password>@psql-kbc-ai-sdlc-
  module4.postgres.database.azure.com:5432/books?sslmode=require
AZURE_OPENAI_ENDPOINT=https://oai-kbc-ai-sdlc-module4.openai.azure.com/
AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY=<key>
AZURE_OPENAI_EMBEDDING_DEPLOYMENT=text-embedding-3-large

~2 min. Brief it and stop. The slide deliberately does not say how. Working out that there is more than one way to hand a capability to an agent is the exercise; naming the routes here removes it.

Three bullets, one click each. Already done, what we want, how long. Nothing else belongs on this slide, and anything you add out loud is a hint.

Point at the second panel once. That is the actual .env.example: the Postgres connection string, the Azure endpoint and key, and the embedding deployment name. It is already filled in on their VM, so this is what it looks like, not something to type. The point that the tool only hands back passages, never an answer, now lives entirely on the “How much should the tool do?” slide, so do not re-make it here.

Practical things they will need, and these are fair to say out loud: the jars are in ~/kbc-saving-streak-seed/tools/, and the tool reads .env from the working directory, then next to the jar, then the jar’s parent directory, with a variable set in the process environment overriding all three. Everything else, let them find.

When someone asks “should this be a skill or a server”, do not answer. Ask which one they would rather hand to the team next door, and walk away. They will pick, and they will have a reason, which is exactly what the debrief needs.

Expect a lopsided finish. The skill route takes about ten minutes, the server route about twenty-five. That is not a flaw in the exercise, it is the first finding, and someone will say it in the debrief. Let them.

If a table is stuck at fifteen minutes, point them at skills. It is the route that always finishes, and a finished skill beats an unfinished server for the discussion.

Open: the corpus sits in Azure Postgres and the query is embedded by Azure OpenAI, so every VM in the room needs outbound 5432 and 443. The VMs' egress IP is not confirmed and neither is whether KBC network policy allows either hop. Until it is tested from a real VM, the whole exercise is one firewall rule away from not running. Module 4 · Exercise

Your turn

30 minutes. Then we compare what everyone did.

~10 seconds, then 30 minutes of quiet. Say the time, say that you will compare afterwards, and get out of the way. Do not add a last piece of advice on your way past this slide.

Put the time on the board, not just in your head. The room needs to see the clock, because the two routes finish at very different points and the people who finished early should be starting the second one rather than waiting.

Circulate, do not present. The trainer's job for the next half hour is to unstick people without telling them which route to take. Questions about the corpus, the jar or the connection are fair to answer directly. Questions about how to expose it are not.

At twenty-five minutes, say there are five left and that an unfinished attempt is fine. The discussion works on what they tried, not on what they shipped.

4 · Trade-offs

How much should the tool do?

You are handing the agent a capability. Does it hand back an answer, or the evidence?

~4 min, and it is a discussion, not a slide. This runs before either door gets walked through, on purpose: what the tool should return is a design question, and it is easier to argue while the mechanics are still out of the way. Three clicks: the left-hand shape, the right-hand shape, then the caption. Put the first one up and ask whether that is what they were handed. It is not. The tool they were given is the right-hand shape: it returns five passages and never composes an answer, and that is true whichever door they built, because both doors call the same search. Ask who noticed, and how many assumed it would answer. That decision was made for them too, they just did not have to see it happen, and most tools arrive with it baked in exactly like this.

The case for the left. One round trip, predictable cost and latency, and you control the model and the prompt so every caller gets the same quality. It is the right shape when the caller is not an agent (a form, a support widget, a batch job), or when you are accountable for the wording that comes out.

The case for the right. The agent already has the codebase, the conversation and the question in front of it. Your tool has none of that, so any answer it composes is composed with less information than the caller had. Returning evidence lets the thing with the most context do the reasoning.

The sentence worth landing: a tool that answers returns an opinion, a tool that retrieves returns evidence. You can check evidence.

Push back on the right-hand one too or it turns into a sermon: it costs a round trip per search, it fills the window with passages, and an agent that can re-query can also re-query five times and get nowhere. That is the failure they will actually meet.

The concrete version of the question: what would it take to make their door hand back a finished answer instead of five passages, and who would then own that prompt and pay for that model? Show of hands for who would add it, then ask both sides why. It is the same argument as the diagram, but about the file on their own screen.

If the room is quiet, ask who would be comfortable putting the left-hand version in front of a customer, and who would be comfortable putting the right-hand one in front of an auditor. Different hands go up, and the discussion runs itself.

Connects toThis is the supervision question from 2.3 and Module 1 again: how much judgement you delegate, and whether you can check the result. Same question, now about a tool instead of a task. The next two slides are the mechanics of whichever answer they picked.

4 · Door one

Door one: a skill

A markdown file that tells the agent when to run something, and how. The something already exists.

.claude/skills/book-search/SKILL.md 
---
name: book-search
description: Search two books about beer
  and brewing. Use when asked about beer,
  ale, brewing methods, the beer trade,
  or how beer was taxed.
---

Run the bundled jar from the repo root:

```bash
java -jar tools/book-search.jar "<question>"
```

It hands back passages, not an answer.
Cite the book each passage came from. If
nothing matches, say so rather than
answering from memory.
Recap: covered in module 2
  • A folder, not a file. SKILL.md plus what it calls, in .claude/skills/.
  • The description is the trigger. Vague description, no match, and nothing tells you it missed.
  • The body waits. Only the description is loaded up front.
  • New here: it needs a shell. The agent reaches this by running something, so the client has to be able to execute.

~3 min. Half the room built this. Walk the file, do not explain markdown.

Spend the time on the description field, not the body. It is the only part with a failure mode that is invisible: a skill that never triggers looks exactly like a skill that does not exist. Read the description on the slide out loud and point at the phrase “use when asked about”. That is the part doing the work, because it is written in the words a person would actually use.

Contrast it with what people write first: “A helpful skill for searching documentation.” Nothing in that sentence overlaps with anything anyone will ever type. That example comes back on the last slide, so plant it here.

The last bullet is the one that decides the argument two slides from now. A skill is instructions plus a script, so the client must be able to execute. Claude Code can. A client without a shell cannot. Do not resolve it here.

Note the relative path in the code block and say you will come back to it. The skill runs from the repo root, so tools/book-search.jar resolves. The next slide has the same jar reached a different way and the relative path breaks there, which is the single most common reason a working server refuses to start in the room.

Connects to2.4 already covered what the always-loaded layer costs, which is why the third bullet gets one line and no more. Do not re-run that argument.

4 · Door two

Door two: a server

The same function, wrapped as a tool and registered with the client. Now it is a process, not a file.

booksearch/mcp/Mcp.java 
// stdout belongs to the transport. Hand it over,
// then point System.out somewhere harmless.
PrintStream realOut = System.out;
System.setOut(new PrintStream(System.err, true));
// our own wrapper round stdin, not System.in raw: it
// sees EOF and holds it until the calls already in
// flight have been answered.
var transport = new StdioServerTransportProvider(
    McpJsonDefaults.getMapper(),
    holdingEof(System.in, doneServing), realOut);

var tool = Tool.builder("search_books", SCHEMA)
    .description(DESCRIPTION).build();  // when to use it

McpServer.sync(transport)
  .serverInfo("book-search", "1.0.0")
  .capabilities(ServerCapabilities.builder()
      .tools(true).build())
  .toolCall(tool, (ex, req) -> handle(req, searcher))
  .build();

doneServing.await();
System.exit(0);  // the client owns the lifetime
  • The description is the trigger. Same job it did in the skill: it is what the model reads to decide.
  • It is always there. The tool definition is registered when the session starts, whether the question ever comes up or not.
  • Nothing needs a shell. The client calls a tool; it does not run your code. Any MCP client can use it.
  • It is a process. Something has to start it, keep it running, and be responsible when it is not.
register it 
$ claude mcp add book-search -- java -jar \
    /home/<user>/workshop/tools/book-search-mcp.jar

Absolute path, always. The client starts the server from a directory nobody chose, so a relative jar path is simply not found.

~3 min. The other half of the room built this, and some of them did not finish. Walk it at a pace that lets the unfinished ones see the whole shape.

The line to point at is the call to search. It is the same BookSearch class, the same SQL and the same five passages that the skill reaches by running the CLI jar. Two jars, one search. Nothing about the retrieval changed between the two doors, only the way it is reached. If that lands, the comparison on the next slide is about distribution and nothing else, which is where you want it.

Bullets three and four are a pair and they pull opposite ways. The server reaches more clients precisely because it is a process, and it is a liability precisely because it is a process. Say both in the same breath.

The first three lines are the ones that cost the room the most time. On stdio the transport owns stdout, and nothing else may touch it: one stray println and the client reads a malformed frame and drops the connection, with no useful error. So you keep a reference to the real stdout, hand that to the transport, and point System.out at stderr so logging is safe again. If anyone had a server that registered and then died, this was almost certainly why.

The second gotcha is the registration line. Absolute path, every time. It is on the slide because roughly half the people who hit it spent ten minutes on it, and because it is the difference between a server that works in their terminal and one that works from the client.

Someone will ask why you would ever bother, given the skill took ten minutes. Do not answer it. Write it on the board and take it into the next slide, because it is the right question and it deserves the room rather than you.

Connects toThe claude mcp add line is the same one from 2.1 of Dataroots' Agentic AI Academy. Worth saying: back then they added someone else's server, and now they have written one.

4 · Trade-offs

Which door, when

Neither is better. They break in different ways, and for different people.

SkillServer
what it isa folder you copya process you run
how it travelsthey take a copy of the filesthey add a command or a URL
who holds the keyswhoever holds the filesyou do, and the caller never sees them
upgrading iteveryone is on their own copyfix it once, everyone has it
who can use itclients that can run a scriptany MCP client
when it breaksit silently never triggersit is down, for everybody

A server is infrastructure and gets treated like it. A skill is a document, and it spreads like one, stale copies included.

Running a serverWhere it runsSuits
local, stdioa subprocess on your machineone person, local data, no auth
remote, HTTPa service you host behind a URLa team, one version, your keys

~5 min. Two reveals: the table, the kicker, then the transports table. Scope was settled three slides ago; this one is only about distribution, so do not let it drift back into what the tool should return.

Do not read the first table. Ask which row surprised them, and let the room argue. The rows are ordered so the argument builds: the first two are mechanics, the middle two are the real content, and the last one is the one nobody thinks about until it happens.

“Who holds the keys” is the row that changes minds. A skill you hand to another team is a connection you have handed to another team. Most people have not thought of a shared folder of files as a credential distribution problem, and it plainly is.

Today's lab makes this row uncomfortably concrete, so use it. The search talks to a Postgres server and to Azure OpenAI, and both sets of credentials live in one .env. Hand someone the skill folder and you have handed them that file, or you have handed them a skill that does not run. Ask the room which of those two they would rather explain. The server route never poses the question, because the credentials stay on the side that runs the process.

The transports table is the answer to “why bother with a server” from the previous slide. Local stdio is roughly a skill with extra steps. Remote HTTP is the version that earns its keep, and it earns it on the two middle rows above: one version, and your credentials.

Where to land it: for one person on one machine, a skill, every time. The moment a second team depends on it, the questions are who is on which version and who gets the keys, and those two questions point at a server.

Connects toThis is Module 3's argument in a different costume: a skill is advice that travels, a hosted server is a thing you control. Say that out loud, because they made the same distinction about hooks and CI checks an hour ago.

Module 4 · When it breaks

When it breaks

Both can fail. Only one of them makes it obvious.

~10 seconds. Say the line and move. It is the turn into the last teaching slide of the day, with only the close after it, and the line does the work on its own: a server that is down announces itself. A skill that never fires does not.

Connects toModule 3 spent its hour on controls that fail loudly. This is the other kind, and it is the note the day ends on.

4 · When it breaks

When the skill does nothing

The usual failure is silence. Nothing errors. The skill never fires, and the agent answers from memory instead.

a skill that will never trigger 
---
name: Book Search
description: A helpful skill for
  searching documentation.
---

Run the search script.

Three faults, and the file is valid YAML with all the required fields. That is what makes it hard.

  1. Is it loaded? ls .claude/skills/*/SKILL.md. Wrong folder is the usual answer.
  2. Invoke it by hand. Works when named but never fires on its own? That is the description, not the code.
  3. Read the description as a stranger. It is matched against what someone types. “Searching documentation” matches nothing.
  4. Then the body. “Run the search script” names no script, no path, no arguments.
  5. Then the run. Relative paths resolve from somewhere you did not expect, and no Bash means nothing runs.

~3 min. The last thing you teach today; only the close comes after it. This is a walk-through, so keep it moving and do not pretend to debug on stage. The broken skill on this slide ships in the lab at lab/module-4/solutions/skill-broken/book-search/SKILL.md, with the walkthrough one level up in lab/module-4/solutions/skill-broken/demo-script.md, so you can run the fix live if the room is ahead of time and you have rehearsed it.

Ask the room to find the faults before revealing the steps. They will get the description one. They usually miss that the body is useless, because it reads like an instruction to a person who already knows where the script is.

The three faults, if nobody gets them: the name is not the lowercase-hyphenated form that matches its folder; the description describes the skill instead of saying when to use it; and the body gives a command nobody can run.

Step two is the one worth remembering and the only one that generalises. Invoking by hand separates “it never triggered” from “it triggered and failed”, and those have nothing in common. Everything else on this list is a checklist; that one is a technique.

Close the module on the silence. A hook that fails is loud and a CI check that fails is louder. That was Module 3. A skill that fails is quiet, and the agent confidently answers anyway. That is the note to end the day on.

Open: this checklist is built from the public Claude Code skills documentation, not from the Anthropic skills course, which is behind a login and could not be read. Check it against the course before this is delivered.

Connects toModule 3, directly. Advice fails silently, gates fail loudly, and that asymmetry is the reason the important rules ended up in CI.

4 · Close

What you can do now

  • Take something that already works and make it reachable by an agent, as a skill or as a server.
  • Choose between them on the two questions that decide it: who holds the keys, and who is on which version.
  • Decide what the tool hands back, an answer or the evidence for one, instead of inheriting whatever it came with.
  • Recognise the quiet failure, and know the order to check things in.

None of this needs a project. The smallest useful version is one skill, in one repository, that encodes something your team already knows.

~1 min. Last slide of the module and of the day. Four clicks and the kicker. Read the bullets quickly, they are the objective from the title slide in past tense, then land the kicker and hand over to the wrap-up.

The kicker is the only part that changes what anyone does on Monday. The risk after an hour on MCP servers and hosting is that the room concludes this is infrastructure work that needs a ticket and a quarter. It is not. One skill in one repository is a real answer, and it is the one most of them should start with.

If you are over time, cut the bullets and say the kicker. It survives on its own; the bullets do not.

Do not add a summary of the whole day here. That is the wrap-up's job at 16:45, and it belongs to whoever is running it.

Connects toThe bullets are the module objective from slide 1, which is worth saying out loud: this is what you said you would be able to do at 15:45.

Duplicate notifications

Learning objective

Trace an agent’s investigation, verify its repair, and assess an independent agent review.

The problem

A balance milestone notification reappears after it is read, even though the balance is unchanged. The existing tests pass.

Your task

  1. Investigate before editingObserve the agent’s searches and tools. Check its assumptions.

  2. Reproduce and explainShow the triggering sequence and explain the cause.

  3. Fix and verifyShow a regression test failing before the fix and passing after it. Preserve legitimate notifications.

  4. Get an independent reviewUse a fresh agent context. Assess its findings and address valid concerns.
